title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
text:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.

"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."

Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.

It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.

For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.

That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.

And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.

His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".

Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.

But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.

It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?

It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.

Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.

Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.

And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.

Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.

Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.

In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.

And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.

The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.

Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.

To some, the trust issue feels existential

"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business.

"It feels like… the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover."

But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.

While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.

And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month.…

title: Why are more roofs not made of solar tiles?
text:
Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.

She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.

For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.

This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.

For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs , external . This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes , external .

Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.

Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.

For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.

Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20–30% since it was established in 2019.

In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.

Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".

Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.

The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."

Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.

She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.

"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.

But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."

Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.

Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.

Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.

Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."

Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.

Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.

While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".

But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.

"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.

While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.

One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.

This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.

This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.

In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.

Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."

Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.

What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.

Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".

Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.

She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."…

title: 'Add me on WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
text:
The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July.

But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and told BBC Radio 4's You and Yours it was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise.

The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog.

The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number.

Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work.

Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages.

"Mostly likely it would be a recruitment scam ," he said.

"They would either put you through to a fake job listing, which might involve some form of money muling. It could look like a completely legitimate job, or something ad hoc, but they might pass criminal funds through your account which can lead to terrible consequences.

"It could also be a simple phishing exercise - criminals send out these messages, and what they really want to know is who's picking up, who's active - that information can be resold on the dark web.

"The possibilities are endless. At the end of the day this is a criminal that has reached out to you and they're trying to defraud you in some way shape or form."

Andy Curry, the ICO's head of criminal investigations, told the BBC he believed the calls were coming from abroad.

"We are trying to find who is behind this, why they're doing it and the impact it's having on members of the public," he said.

The number of complaints received by the ICO would only be a small proportion of the totals affected, he said.

"We think there are probably millions of people who are receiving these messages, which appear to us to be largely indiscriminate.

"I've had them, my colleague who's leading the investigation has had them. It's likely to be tip of the iceberg."

'I lost my savings after a job interview scam'

Rise in reports of 'shameful' recruitment scams

Fell said that mobile companies were "working on a range of fronts" to tackle the influx of automated calls.

This includes sending intelligence reports to the regulator Ofcom, working with law enforcement, and liaising with Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because if someone does follow up on the request to add the number to the encrypted platform, "any dialogue that happens between you and the criminal then can't be investigated any further".

A WhatsApp spokesman said there were features in place to protect its users from scam calls, including silencing calls from unknown numbers. He also said WhatsApp banned millions of accounts each year for "malicious behaviours", such as bulk account registration or automated messaging.

While these calls typically appear to be from a UK mobile number, Fell said these numbers will be imitated, or spoofed, by the criminals behind the scam.

Last November, the UK government promised , external that call spoofing would be eliminated within a year.

A Home Office spokesman said the government was taking "robust action" to tackle scams.

"We remain committed to delivering the Telecommunications Charter, alongside industry, by November," he added.

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
author: Guardian sport
text:
Michael Carrick is wary of ‘Dr Tottenham’, Oliver Glasner returns to Selhurst Park and will Manchester City summon a siege mentality at Anfield?

Premier League top scorers | View the league table

Declan Rice’s future role in England’s midfield was questioned by Gary Lineker after Alex Scott’s impressive first senior international start in the 7-0 thrashing of Croatia. But the decision to withdraw from Thomas Tuchel’s squad in an attempt to manage his workload made sense after Rice had only three weeks off post-World Cup before returning to pre-season training. The 27-year-old has struggled with persistent back problems after suffering a hamstring injury last December and Mikel Arteta will hope that the rest has done Rice – who is thought to be close to agreeing a lucrative new contract at the Emirates – the world of good as they prepare to resume the defence of their Premier League title against Leeds on Saturday. Ed Aarons

Several Aston Villa players shone for their countries during the international window but one of those who stayed with the club may have made the biggest impression on Unai Emery. Villa’s remaining squad went to Spain for a mid-season training camp, including Alejandro Garnacho, whose last cap for Argentina was almost two years ago. Garnacho has been lesser-spotted in a Villa shirt, playing just 31 minutes as a substitute, but scored in both of Villa’s friendlies during the break, against Southampton and Sevilla. The 22-year-old, who joined Villa on loan from Chelsea in the summer with a conditional obligation, was an unused substitute for their past matches but is he now primed to affect games? Villa are hopeful Emery has unlocked Garnacho, who has struggled for form since leaving Manchester United . “Ready now!” Garnacho posted on social media last weekend and Villa will hope that is the case. Ben Fisher

With Eli Junior Kroupi, Amine Adli, Veljko Milosavljevic and Julián Araujo yet to feature this season due to injury, Marco Rose must have been tearing his remaining hair out upon learning Alex Scott got hurt on England duty and will be out of action for two months. Sitting 17th and still searching for their first league win, the German’s side squandered nine points from winning positions in four of their first five games – and it was the 23-year-old who was central in ensuring Bournemouth had those leads in the first place. With just 55 minutes of football behind him this season, it seems unlikely Alex Toth will get the nod to replace Scott when Bournemouth travel to Chelsea with the older, more experienced Ryan Christie available and in good form. But having forced his way into the Hungary starting lineup during the international break it would be no surprise to see the 20-year-old get more minutes with a view to being used far more often given his side’s gruelling schedule of nine matches in the next month. Barry Glendenning

Ipswich’s place in mid-table, their total of six points, came via victories over Sunderland and Crystal Palace . Gary O’Neil’s team were presented with a tough opening schedule, and while defeated by Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, their manager has not allowed those reverses to dilute team spirit. Speaking to the media following the home defeat by Liverpool , O’Neil painted an ultra-positive picture that defied most observers’ view of a game beyond his team’s reach from the early stages. Thus far, a successful strategy, certainly by comparison to early season at winless Fulham. Like O’Neil, Álvaro Arbeloa is new to his job. An improved performance in the draw against United did not result in a victory Fulham deserved, though there were signs of the progressive, attacking football the arrival of the former Real Madrid interim promised. Much of the burden has fallen on Josh King, the teenager building on last year’s breakthrough season. John Brewin

Still in the Carabao Cup, with a Europa League campaign to negotiate and just four points acquired from their opening five Premier League excursions, the games are about to start coming thick and fast for a Sunderland side whose ability to cope with such a hectic schedule remains to be seen. Having lost Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey to hamstring injuries during the international break, Régis Le Bris will have to reshuffle his pack against a free-scoring Brighton side who make the 700-mile round trip to Wearside for their first game since embarrassing Arsenal three weeks ago. While Wilson Isidor will almost certainly deputise for Brobbey, Ballard’s centre-back berth will be filled by either Omar Alderete or Nordi Mukiele. Having shipped five last time out against Manchester City , a Sunderland defence that had looked conspicuously porous in the early stages of this season will need all their focus if they are to stop the gallop of a team that have already scored 16 goals. BG .

If “Dr Tottenham” is a thing, Manchester United possess their own healing powers for opponents. Self-harm is a factor too. They rolled out the welcome mat to Premier League newcomers Hull on opening day and Brighton were ushered back into a Carabao Cup tie . In United’s final game before the international break flagging Fulham were able to restore some faith, their goal via slapstick defending from Lisandro Martínez and Senne Lammens. Can Old Trafford, where fans will have regulatory matters at City to celebrate, lift the gloom for Tottenham? This season, like last season and the one before that, Spurs have assumed the mantle of crisis club, a status Michael Carrick’s January arrival temporarily removed from United. Lose to Tottenham, and the crisis prefix is likely to be reattached. Tottenham have done damage before. In September 2024, a 3-0 Spurs win at Old Trafford began Erik ten Hag’s hurtle towards the exit. Losing the Europa League final started Ruben Amorim’s downward spiral. Carrick beware? JB…

title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring programme
text:
Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.

Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.

Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable companies in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."

Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.

"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.

He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.

Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.

The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.

The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped , external at 85,000 per year.

A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.

Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.

The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.

She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.

According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary , external for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.

"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.

Satya Nadella, Microsoft's long-time chief executive, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.

Introducing Nadella during the event, Trump said the White House was "honoured" to be awarding the medal to him and that it was "so well-deserved".

Other tech industry figures to receive medals from Trump were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Michael Dell.

Nadella and most of the other medal recipients were also present at other recent White House events, including a lunch on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.

Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.

"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.

He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.

Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating , external that grace period altogether.

Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.

None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.

The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.

The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.

During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified , external more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

title: SpaceX calls for better coordination in orbit after near-misses with Starlink
author: Stephen Clark
text:
Space has plenty of room for more megaconstellations, but only if all operators are willing to share information about where their satellites are and where they're going, a top executive at SpaceX and its AI subsidiary said this week.

Michael Nicolls, SpaceX's vice president for Starlink and president of Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company, xAI, used a presentation Tuesday at the International Astronautical Congress in Turkey as a clarion call for improved data-sharing among satellite operators.

SpaceX's Starlink constellation now has more than 11,000 satellites, about two-thirds of all active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit. Radars and telescopes routinely track thousands more pieces of space junk.

title: Mikayla Harvey and Oliver Bleddyn set to strengthen Jayco-AlUla women’s and men’s rosters for next two years
author: Owen Rogers
text:
GreenEdge Cycling have announced two additions to their structure, with New Zealander Mikayla Harvey joining the Liv-AlUla-Jayco women’s set up and Australian track star Oliver Bleddyn arriving at the men’s Jayco-AlUla squad.

Both riders have signed with the Australian WorldTour teams on two-year contracts, taking them to the end of 2028.

While Bleddyn is best known as a track rider, where his successes include a gold medal in the Team Pursuit at the Paris Olympic Games, the 24-year-old has plenty of experience on the road. This year, he was second in the time trial at both the Australian and Oceania championships and joined the team as a stagiaire with Jayco-AlUla at the start of August. Since then he completed the Arctic Race of Norway, but has struggled since, finishing only one of seven late-season Italian Classics.

"I’m really excited about what next year can bring. There are some great opportunities ahead and I’m super keen to make the most of them," Belddyn said in a team press release.

"The Tour Down Under would definitely be a special race for me to do. To race at home with this team is an opportunity I’d be really excited about."

The team’s head of performance, Gene Bates, is looking forward to working with Bleddyn, saying, "he has got a huge engine".

"He is a great and enthusiastic young rider and is also gaining a lot of experience on the road, riding as a stagiaire with the team this second half of the 2026 season. We are confident Oliver will be a great addition to the team in many different roles," Bates said.

Harvey arrives after two years at SD Worx-Protime, and similar stints at UAE Team ADQ and Canyon-SRAM already behind the 28-year-old climber. Working mostly as a domestique, Harvey is able to take her leaders deep into hilly finals, and has the engine to bring breakaways back on flat days.

Though she began this year with second place in both the time trial and road race at the New Zealand nationals, she didn’t start her European season until the Ardennes Classics in April. A crash took her out of the Giro d’Italia Women in June, since then she’s struggled to regain consistency, crashing out of the Classic Lorient Agglomération and the Faun Tour Femmes, where she suffered a concussion.

"I am already looking forward to next season," Harvey said. "I am a rider that has experienced a lot, and I feel like I can add this to the team. Alongside this, I am a rider that is not afraid of trying something and being outside my comfort zone. I love attacking and dynamic racing. Especially looking for breakaways and escaping from the peloton."

The team expect her to play a big role in hilly races, including the chance to race for herself.

"Over the past few seasons, she has played an important support role, but with us she will also have the chance to race for her own ambitions again," said Head Sport Director Wim Stroetinga. "We strongly believe she has the talent and ability to be competing at the front of races and fighting for victories, and we are excited to help her take that next step."

Neither men’s nor women’s programmes have been especially active in this summer’s transfer market, Bleddyn joining Will Holmes as the only two signings to the men’s squad so far. At the same time, not only are they about to lose Luka Mezgec and Luke Durbridge to retirement, and Mauro Schmid to Pinarello-Q36.5, a number of other riders are still to announce their futures with the team.

On the women’s side, Harvey is the only new arrival revealed so far, though Erin Boothman has been promoted from the structure’s Continental development team.

title: Six-day American Criterium Cup summer schedule confirmed for 2027 while USA CRITS taking shape for spring - North American Roundup
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
For a third year, the American Criterium Cup will include six stops across the central and western US to determine overall individual and team champions among well-established criterium events. Races will take place from June 11 to September 5, with Saint Francis Tulsa Tough establishing the first leaderboards in Oklahoma and the finale at the Bommarito Audi West County Gateway Cup in Missouri.

The Tour of America's Dairyland will host the second race in Milwaukee, Wisconsin on June 26, with the third race, the Bailey & Glasser LLP Twilight Criterium in Boise, Idaho on July 10. After the August 1 Fulton Market race with Chicago GRIT, the series swings back to the west for the Salt Lake Criterium in Utah on August 7, and then a month later, the winners will be decided in St. Louis.

The 2027 season marks the seventh for the ACC. Last year each event offered a $16,000 prize purse for pro women and pro men, with the series paying out an additional $44,000 to series winners across several classifications. Plans for any live streaming broadcasts have not been confirmed.

Skylar Schneider dominated the women's competition this year, holding the red leader's jersey from start to finish, while Justin Williams made it a L39ION of Los Angeles sweep in the individual rankings taking the men's top spot. L39ION also won the team titles, the men's team title decided on a tiebreaker against Team Cadence Cyclery p/b Waldo Racing at the final event in St. Louis.

Claudia Marcks (Pedla Racing Division) took the sprint classification across the six races by a single point over Holly Breck (L39ION of Los Angeles), while the men's green jersey as best sprinter went to Owen Gillott (Chaney Windows and Doors Big Shark p/b Pastaria).

USA CRITS, the spring block of one-day races in the southeastern region of the US, will return for an 18th edition in 2027, anchored by the Athens Orthopedic Clinic Twilight in Georgia on Saturday, April 17.

Races in Greenville, Spartanburg, Suwanee and Winston Salem were expected to return following Athens, with additional events still "being nailed down" to bring the series to eight total, according to Gene Dixon, founder of USA CRITS and owner of series producer Swagger LLC.

The bulk of the calendar will focus on races across Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, the final calendar set in the coming weeks.

Dixon said the emphasis was to provide a compact 30-day window to simplify travel for riders and teams, especially those traveling from outside the US. A similar prize purse to this year is expected, totalling $200,000 for individual races and overall series classifications with equal payouts among the men's and women's elite riders. All USA CRITS races will provide live streaming, produced by Swagger.

Liza Ray (Kingdom Elite Racing) and Leonel Rodriguez (MC Cycling Team) won the individual titles in 2026.

Next year's Amazon Armed Forces Cycling Classic, June 5-6, will introduce a UCI 1.2-level road race as part of two days of elite men's racing and continue with back-to-back criteriums for elite women. Organisers confirmed that the equal prize purse of more than $30,000 would remain in place.

Last week reported that the UCI calendar had added two new men's races to the 2027 America Tour, Battenkill in New York on May 22 and the Amazon Armed Forces cycling Classic Capitol Cup in Washington, D.C. The long-running AFCC weekend will continue with a full schedule of USA Cycling-sanctioned criteriums, Capitol Cup on Saturday and Clarendon Cup on Sunday.

"This change reflects the vision we share with our partner Amaury Sport Organisation (A.S.O.) for the event's future," said Robert Laybourn, president of Arlington Sports, Inc, and the event race director.

"Every major decision we make is guided by documented metrics and data. The event will continue to evolve and be refined as our budget and other constraints allow, pursuing changes that offer proven value to its growth, success and long-term sustainability."

Organisers at Arlington Sports have not published a schedule yet, however, they have indicated to that the men's course will take place on a 20km (12.5-mile) circuit, the exact distance is yet to be determined. The race is expected follow directly after the early Saturday start of the Challenge Ride, where non-competitive riders have a three-hour window to complete up to five laps of the same circuit.

Then the event will showcase the elite women as the final action of the day, held on the same 1.4km course as last year situated in front of the US Capitol building and the National Mall.

Clarendon Cup events, now in a 29th year, will return to nearby Arlington, Virginia on Sunday. Last year omnium titles for the two days of racing were won by Marlies Mejías (Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY28/Deloitte) and Brody McDonald (Modern Adventure Pro Cycling).

title: Judge weighs if Trump can charge $100K for early access to Truth Social posts
author: Ashley Belanger
text:
Likely in the next few weeks, a federal judge will decide if Donald Trump can become the first president to personally profit from selling early access to government information in his social media posts.

At a hearing Wednesday, Department of Justice civil attorney Brantley Mayers argued that there was no conflict whatsoever with Trump charging up to $100,000 monthly for instant API access to Truth Social posts that often break news from his administration.

Trump is the largest stakeholder and majority owner of Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company that owns Truth Social, and the value of the API access comes largely from Trump’s role as president.

title: Trump Mobile hack and apparent lack of FCC authorization raise security alarms
author: Jon Brodkin
text:
Trump Mobile apparently failed to obtain necessary authorizations to operate the international calling portion of its phone service, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) wrote in a letter to the company today.

Her letter said Trump Mobile also doesn't appear to have submitted a required plan for fighting robocalls. Trump Mobile's key business partner, Liberty Mobile Wireless, did make a robocall database filing, but it was not complete, Hassan said.

Hassan's letter raised questions about Trump Mobile's security related to a report that hackers stole personal data of 3,615 customers and Trump Mobile's previous confirmation that a vendor it uses exposed customers' personal data on the Internet. Hassan alleged that Trump Mobile failed to follow multiple FCC filing rules that are supposed to help ensure the security of mobile services.

title: Feds get ready to rewrite car headlight rules
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
text:
One of the regulations that make vehicles in the US different from those in Europe or Japan is our headlight rules. They’re laid out in the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), and changing them is—or used to be—a lengthy, laborious process, which is a major reason automotive lighting technology has lagged in the US. But the current administration says it’s time for “bolstering driver safety, slashing red tape, and embracing new technologies,” so it’s going to start a negotiated rulemaking process to rewrite the regulations to suit 2026.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Jonathan Morrison said. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”

title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
author: South West News Service
text:
Free-roaming Aldabra population thrives on Indian Ocean atoll due to decades-long recovery programme

A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey , led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.

“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

title: RIP Margaret Hamilton, whose code saved the Apollo 11 Moon landing
author: Jennifer Ouellette
text:
Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term "software engineering" and led the development of onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo program in the 1960s, died last week at the age of 90. A recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Hamilton was also immortalized as a LEGO minifig the following year—part of the "Women of NASA" set that also included astronauts Mae Jemison and Sally Ride.

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer—to say she was ahead of her time—would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck , interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.”

Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. The plan was for her to work until he finished his law degree, after which he would support her through graduate school to earn a PhD in mathematics.

title: Evenepoel and Del Toro the favourites, but Il Lombardia is wide open – Analysing the contenders
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
The final Monument of the 2026 season, Il Lombardia , is upon us and we have a fantastic race in prospect thanks to a fascinating array of contenders, who we're going to delve into right here.

We've been adjusting to a Pogačar-less racing scene in recent weeks, and for all that it's a shame to have the world's biggest star on the sidelines, the racing has undeniably been more open, tactical, and interesting as a result.

That's what we're expecting to see again on Saturday, at a 120th edition of the Race of the Falling Leaves that follows the Bergamo to Como direction on a 239km route with a finale over the Madonna del Ghisallo, San Fermo della Battaglia, and Civiglio climbs.

We arguably have two top favourites – though neither so superior as Pogačar – and a rich array of names who will all feel they have a shot at a Monument on Saturday afternoon.

After winning the European road race title , the Belgian has steadied the ship that listed so dramatically in the World Championship, and as such he starts as one of the top two favourites. As Worlds underlined, Evenepoel is a rider who can blow extremely hot and extremely cold. A one-pitch, know-what-you're-getting Pogačar he is not, but then again, that's part of what makes him such a compelling bike rider.

In a Pogačar-less world, Evenepoel – a former world champion, two-time winner of Liège-Bastogne-Liège and five-time winner of the Clásica San Sebastián – ought to be the next man up. 12 months ago, he soloed to second place behind Pogačar rather convincingly, as he did repeatedly last autumn. But despite bouncing back from that off-day at Worlds, you sense Evenepoel is not quite at the height of his powers.

The Europeans felt like a good example of a race he might have won solo at his peak. Indeed, he had to outsprint Giulio Ciccone for the second time in just a few weeks. Now, Evenepoel's sprint is an underrated weapon that only broadens the way in which he can win these big races, but you can't help but feel that the more we've been impressed by it, the more we've seen it in action, and the less that means he's actually been able to get away.

Even so, he remains one of the very top favourites to finally win a race that he looked like he might have won as a 20-year-old in 2020.

The rainbows may be wrapped around the torso of Brandon McNulty, and while the US rider will have more freedom than if Pogačar were present, it's Isaac del Toro who represents the best shot for UAE Team Emirates and a joint favourite alongside Evenepoel.

Del Toro has all the tools to win this race. As the Tour de France runner-up, he has the climbing legs. As the winner of nearly every late-season Italian classic last year, he knows what he's doing in this punchy part of the world. And as the winner of the GP de Montréal in a sprint, he has the finishing speed to win if he has company.

Del Toro has had a remarkable season in which he has won three WorldTour stage races, finished on the podium of his first Tour de France, and won a WorldTour one-dayer at Montreal. His performance at the World Championships in the same location was widely debated and shot through with allegations, and while we will take his ride at face value, there were tactical question marks that – like we saw at the Giro last year – could do with being ironed out.

But on his day he is just the complete package, an electric racer, and he has a huge opportunity here to take the biggest win of his career so far.

It would be rude not to give the world champion his own section. After all, Brandon McNulty's Worlds win , though highly tactical, was no stroke of fortune. He has largely operated as a domestique, but the immense talent that was evident so early in his career has never been far from the surface, and he had racked up a very respectable palmarès even before the world title.

Since he pulled on that rainbow jersey, he has looked invigorated. Some of it might have something to do with Pogačar's recent absence, but he's been launching attacks left, right, and centre in a sign that the jersey is not weighing him down with any sort of onus of suddenly winning all the time now, but rather giving him a boost of confidence and a spring in his step.

It will be interesting to see how he dovetails with Del Toro. The Mexican might be the standout favourite, but Pogačar is not back yet, and while that's the case there's room for McNulty to go after this race, and perhaps make a bit of a statement over his status in the pecking order at UAE.

The Frenchman takes to Lombardia to round out one of the most extraordinary seasons we've seen in recent years, one in which he rose to the top echelon of the sport and became the most hyped man in professional cycling.

Seixas looks likely to win this race in the future – you could say that about a lot of races – and while it wouldn't be a total shock to see him do it this year, excitement surrounding the recently-turned 20-year-old has dampened somewhat compared to his blistering Spring.

Back then, he was genuinely looking like the second-best rider in the world with runner-up finishes behind Pogačar at Strade Bianche and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, either side of a complete evisceration of the Itzulia Basque Country field. He was fast-tracked into his Tour de France debut, and since then a touch off the gloss has worn off, with a more subdued racing style and a level just a notch lower.

That's no slant on Seixas. Fourth on debut at the Tour de France at 19 is still otherworldly, and he only lost the GP de Montréal in a sprint against Isaac del Toro. But the World Championships, where he cramped in the finale, highlighted some - to be expected - limitations, and also the level of pressure he puts on his own shoulders, berating himself for riding like a schoolkid.

However it lands, and he has all the tools to win it, Lombardia represents the final act of a breakthrough season and the start of a reset that may well lead to a different beast in 2027.

Ciccone has shown his one-day shape is where it needs to be in recent weeks. As at the Europeans, he was out-sprinted only by Evenepoel at the end of the QP de Québec, and he was sixth at Worlds after looking momentarily like he might make his way across to McNulty alongside Tom Pidcock on the final lap.

It's hard to see him winning in an outright sprint against some of the riders on this list, but as shown by the way he took the fight to Evenepoel at Europeans, he has the race craft to make different things happen. When he's in this form and this mood, Ciccone is fantastic to watch. And after the Europeans, he may even be riding with a little extra fire in his belly, which, for a rider who has always ridden on emotion, might just make an all-important difference.

You never quite know what you're going to get with Tom Pidcock, which is probably why he's so exciting to watch. On his day, he's world-class, as evidenced by a palmarès that includes Strade Bianche, Amstel Gold Race, and a Grand Tour podium, along with all his off-road titles.

His challenge to Pogačar at Milan-San Remo this Spring was another reminder of the levels he can reach on his day. But he can also look pretty ordinary, make mistakes, or fade away in big races.

It can be hard to read his form, but it looks pretty good. He had a subdued Tour de France and then won the Mountain Bike Worlds, so it's been a tight one to adjust for a late-season full of hilly one-day races, but he seems to have done a decent job, winning on comeback at the GP Industria & Artigianato and featuring prominently in every race since, with podiums at Tre Valli Varesine and Giro dell'Emilia.

He was also top 10 at the GPs de Québec and Montréal, and in the World Championships, where he was one of the very strongest in the group behind McNulty.

He was also the most generous, and that's probably the most reliable thing about Pidcock – that he'll commit and go all-in for the win rather than playing games and riding for the podium. With no co-leader on his level at Pinarello Q36.5, it leaves him slightly exposed, and he may find himself in awkward situations on Saturday once again. But if he can take that small step towards his sparkling best, then he is well in with a shout of a first Monument title.

Matteo Jorgenson has looked incredibly strong in recent weeks – just a vision of perfect posture and, in contrast to some of the more spritely climbers on this list, pure seated horsepower. The World Championships would indicate that Jorgenson would thrive in a more grinding, attritional affair, but he still had the punch to follow Tom Pidcock's decisive acceleration at Tre Valli Varesine.

The big weakness in Jorgenson's arsenal is his sprint finish. He barely has one. So he'd need to win alone. And that's certainly not out of the question given the lack of Pogačar and given the potential room for tactical manoeuvre.

In that respect, we need to highlight Visma's two-pronged approach, with Davide Piganzoli another credible candidate for the Lombardia title. More on the young Italian in a minute, but what's clear already from the past few races is how well they've combined. Piganzoli, of course, won the Giro dell'Emilia, and much like Brandon McNulty's world title, it was massively aided and abetted by Jorgenson's presence, strength, and actions in the group behind.

The pair both attacked in the finale of Tre Valli Varesine, and this time it was Jorgenson who got to play the finale, but was third in the three-man sprint. Is Jorgenson just the perfect second fiddle, or can he become the main man in Como?

We've mentioned some of Piganzoli's results, and his collaboration with Jorgenson, but the 24-year-old Italian deserves his own slot on this list. He has had a fantastic breakthrough season, shining as the top mountain domestique at the Giro d'Italia won by his teammate Jonas Vingegaard, and finishing eighth himself in the process.

He was then drafted into the Tour de France squad late on, and in truth he was unable to reach his Giro form at any point during the race, but still ended up in 14th place overall. He went on to win the Tour of Luxembourg – his second stage race title of the season after the Route d'Occitanie – before his brilliantly-taken solo victory at the Giro dell'Emilia, which has propelled him up the list of contenders for Il Lombardia.

Are we getting carried away here? I'm not so sure. The 20-year-old Belgian just won his first pro race, at Tre Valli Varesine , outsprinting two riders higher up this list in the process. With that, he has put himself at the forefront of our minds ahead of Il Lombardia.

And yet, he is far from a reliable contender for this race. For starters, it's his first Monument, his first real test in a race as heavy as this in terms of distance and climbing. Secondly, the stunning talent that Widar showed in the U23 ranks has only come through in patches this season (which is absolutely fair enough). Thirdly, Widar is more of a puncheur than a climber, and while the climbs individually suit him, it's far from a given he'll stay the course here.

That said, it was only recently that he was the best of the rest behind Pogačar on a big mountain stage of the Vuelta to Andorra. And when it comes to a sprint, he showed in mid-week that he has one of the best. He may have surprised Pidcock at Tre Valli, but the Briton responded quickly and got nowhere near him.

It could go one of two ways, and while he might fall away completely, you wouldn't count him out of being in podium contention.

Ben Healy hasn't hit the heights he did during his fantastic run of form in 2025, but there have been signs that he's getting back there after a difficult 2026 campaign. The Irishman was 8th at GP de Montreal, 10th at Worlds, sixth at Giro dell'Emilia, and in the main group at Tre Valli Varesine.…

title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
text:
Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.

Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis , she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.

"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."

She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."

Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.

"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.

"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."

His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.

On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".

Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.

Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.

Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday .

Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.

Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.

When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.

"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."

Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.

In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.

Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.

A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.

Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.

However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.

He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.

Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.

"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."

The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.

The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.

There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.

Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.

Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.

Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.

However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.

That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.

"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."

He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.

Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.…

title: Ticket rises and more TV packages - why is price of sport increasing?
text:
At least £115 to watch a day of the Ashes in Birmingham - unless you are an Edgbaston member.

A minimum of £255 for a standard seat at the Wimbledon singles finals.

Prices starting from £289 for general admission to the British Grand Prix at Silverstone on raceday.

Those are the ticket fees British sports fans have been told a single adult must pay if they want to attend some of the country's most beloved sports events in 2027.

The cost of entry to elite sport in the UK has risen sharply in the 2020s, but attendances across the majority of sports are as strong as ever.

Even for armchair fans watching at home, the breadth and expense of television subscriptions can be a barrier to accessing sport.

So what exactly is behind the rise in prices, can the increases possibly be justified and what does it all mean for fans?

In a new BBC Radio 5 Live programme - The Price of Our Sport - BBC Sport has taken a look.

Fans reacted with anger when some of the ticket price rises for major events next year were announced earlier this summer.

The increase in Ashes ticket prices is stark - the minimum price the last time Edgbaston held a Test in 2023 was £65, a rise of £50 to £115 in just four years. Admission to other venues, including The Oval, is even higher.

Last time out in Australia, some seats were sold to fans at all five venues for between £16 and £22.

At Wimbledon next year, the most expensive standard seat for both the men's and women's singles finals will be £400, £50 more than 2026, and more than double the cost from 2017.

That still makes Wimbledon the cheapest of the four Grand Slams, but even a Centre Court ticket for the middle Saturday of the tournament now costs at least £130.

General admission for Grand Prix Sunday at Silverstone is up to £289 from £189 in 2021, while the cheapest allocated seat now costs at least £609, up from £276 five years ago.

And general admission to the 2027 Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, in the Republic of Ireland, will cost €499 (£434), compared with up to €260 (£220) in Italy in 2023.

And other events which took place this year laid bare just how much more fans are being charged.

Fans paid £150 to attend a day of The Open at Royal Birkdale earlier this year, compared to £95 at St Andrews in 2022.

Prices for the FA Cup final varied from £50 to £285 in 2026, compared with £50 to £120 in 2016.

"It's just ludicrous," says Lee Hanlon, an England cricket fan who lives close to Edgbaston, but has decided not to attend next summer's Ashes because of the price rise.

"I'm angry. It seems like a lot of the normal cricket fans have been priced out. It seems like just people with money are going now.

"The increase is just too much. I find it upsetting."

But for event organisers, the prices chime with wider trends.

"We exist in an experience economy - we have definitely seen a subtle shift in the value people are placing on belonging, on the atmosphere you can be part of when you attend a live experience," says Mark Darbon, chief executive of the R&A, which operates golf's Open Championship.

"So when we set our prices we start by looking at some of the other major sporting events and benchmark ourselves, on price and value for money, by looking at what others are delivering."

In a poll on the BBC Sport website, 95% of respondents voted that tickets for the 2027 Ashes were too expensive.

A spokesperson for Edgbaston said: "Our entry-level ticket prices roughly match inflation compared to the last time Australia visited Edgbaston in 2023 - but like the rest of the country, we're battling increased costs and trying to manage these wherever we can."

Whether prices are set by governing bodies or the stadiums, the costs of putting on a major sports event include things like utilities, staffing, technology, insurance and marketing.

The Open offers half-price tickets for attendees aged 16-24, and free tickets for children.

"Ticketing revenue generates less than 20% of our total revenue from The Open," Darbon says.

"We have seen really significant cost inflation in recent years. It now costs us 25% more than it did five or six years ago to host The Open - that could be £10-12m in incremental costs. We have to cover those costs."

Many prestige events and newly built venues also include an increased proportion of hospitality ticketing, which can drive up costs for fans wanting standard tickets.

"We are seeing more and more regular people willing to pay for a special experience at sport," says Richard Flint, chairman of Seat Unique, an online platform specialising in hospitality and VIP ticketing for events.

"Corporate boxes are being broken down more and more into individual seats, so it's less about people taking 10 of their colleagues and more about a couple, or four people, going together.

"[Teams and leagues] want to grow their revenue off the back of it, undeniably. Premium is much more open to people or go to one or two games a year, or who have travelled from abroad to come.

"Sometimes stadiums need updating and the revenue from premium ticketing can help fund a new stadium or new stand, so there are benefits to the everyday fan."

In a world with increasingly volatile economics and changing consumer habits, broadcasting live sport has been one of the more reliable ways for companies to generate revenue.

And live sport - and entertainment - is one of the few industries whose financial success is unlikely to be significantly compromised by artificial intelligence in the coming years.

That means more and more companies have taken an interest in buying the rights to show sports events, which means more TV subscriptions than ever before are necessary for fans wanting to watch all of the action.

A football fan in the UK, for example, must subscribe to Sky Sports, TNT Sports, Amazon Prime and Premier Sports, if they want to watch all of the matches across the Premier League, Champions League and Scottish Premiership.…

title: Egan Bernal says his 'intention is to start the upcoming season' but admits question marks over his future
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Egan Bernal has stated his intention "to start the upcoming season", but the winner of the 2019 Tour de France has admitted there are question marks surrounding his future.

Bernal posted a personal statement on his social media on Thursday, after the journalist Daniel Benson reported on his Substack that he was weighing up his future, including the possibility of retiring at the end of this year.

Bernal, who confirmed he had ended his 2026 season after the Tour de France, indicated that he will race on into 2027, but his statement was hardly categorical.

"First of all, I am under contract with the team until the end of 2029, and right now, my intention is to start the upcoming season," Bernal wrote, confirming that his season.

Further down his statement, he added: "I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now."

The 29-year-old has been with Netcompany-Ineos since 2018, winning the Tour the following year and the Giro d’Italia in 2021. He has also taken victories at Paris-Nice, the Tour de Suisse and others.

However, a training crash in January 2022, while training at home in Colombia, left him with career-threatening injuries, including a punctured lung, a broken rib and a broken leg, and he was away from racing for eight months. Since returning in August 2022 he has only won four times, three of those in the Colombian national championships. And while he occasionally shows flashes of his old brilliance, he is unable to compete with the current crop of GC stars.

"After so many years dedicated to cycling, I feel I have given the best years of my life to the sport - both as a cyclist and as a person," Bernal wrote.

"I have made sacrifices I never imagined, won races that once seemed like impossible dreams, and experienced both incredible highs and very difficult lows; yet today I can look back with peace of mind, proud of everything I have done and achieved, with no regrets.

"Over time, I have also learned that this sport isn’t just about results, victories, or sacrifices. It is also about enjoying the journey and finding the motivation to keep doing what you love.

"This year, I decided to end my season after the Tour de France. I felt I needed some time for myself - to rest, disconnect a little and regain the sense of calm that can sometimes be lost amidst the relentless pace of competition.

"I have spoken with the team and the people around me, and we are alone the same page: I want to give myself the time and space needed to face what lies ahead with the same conviction and dedication I have always had.

"I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now. For now, I want to enjoy the present, experience this moment calmly, and let time take its course."

title: Plans to shut Marston's Brewery in Burton revealed
text:
Marston's Brewery could close in Burton-upon-Trent, under plans revealed by its owners.

Carlsberg Britvic said it was proposing to shut the facility together with its primary logistics operation based at that site next summer. About 310 people are affected.

Burton-upon-Trent's connections with the brewing industry date back centuries, with the firm describing its own history and legacy in the town as "iconic".

However, it said the "stark reality" was that UK cask ale volumes had more than halved in less than a decade and "this trend looks set to continue across the UK".

The company said "priority brands" including Hobgoblin, McEwan's and Brooklyn were expected to remain in its portfolio, but it is unclear where they will be brewed.

Other, smaller brands could find a home under specialist or local brewers, the firm said.

Some have described Burton as the "beer capital of England", and at its height more than 30 breweries once operated from there.

The Staffordshire town's connection with beer dates back to the 11th Century when monks first started brewing, and Marston's own links to Burton date back more than 200 years.

Camra chairman Ash Corbett-Collins, who grew up in Burton, said statements from Carlsberg about understanding the importance of the brewery to the town "come far too little too late for most people".

"This announcement is an absolute disgrace, and the latest in a string of actions that show how little they care about our brewing heritage or the nation's drinkers."

But he agreed "with Carlsberg on one thing", adding the "time is right to think about alternative, independent, brewers who are willing to become custodians of Carlsberg's cask brands".

Carlsberg Britvic said it told colleagues and trade union partners the news earlier on Thursday.

CEO Paul Davies said the proposal was "by no means a reflection on any of our people, and every effort will be made to help them through this period of uncertainty".

He added Marston's Brewery and the primary logistics operation were expected to continue to operate "during the transition period, while the company works through the detail of the consultation".

"As and when key decisions are taken over the coming months, we will share further information with the industry, but always with our colleagues first."

Davies said it was important to ensure the firm's portfolio was focused "where consumers are today, and where customer demand is growing".

He added: "That said, smaller ale brands are much loved by select consumers, and we will do everything we can to ensure they thrive under more specialist or local ownership in the future."

It is not the first big brewing firm to move operations in the West Midlands.

Banks's Brewery pulled production out of Wolverhampton in 2025, after 150 years, moving it to Burton.

Carlsberg Marston's Brewing Company (CMBC) had announced in 2024 that the Burton facility would close as part of a company restructuring.

That year, Carlsberg acquired Marston's PLC's remaining 40% shareholding in CMBC, giving Carlsberg full ownership of the brewing business, including Marston's Brewery and its portfolio of beer brands.

Hospitality firm Marston's PLC is now a completely separate operation. It runs more than 1,300 pubs across the UK from its base in Wolverhampton and is unaffected by Thursday's news.

Burton beer is known for its earthy, eggy smell - known in brewing circles as "Burton snatch" - a sure sign of the ale's quality and provenance.

This is created by the water trickling through unusually thick bands of gypsum under the town, before resting in underground aquifers.

Staffordshire County Council's leader, Reform's Martin Murray, said British beer was famous across the world and over the years much of that had come out of Burton.

"For us to lose that heritage personally saddened me greatly," he said.

The leader of the opposition at the authority, Conservative Philip White, said the "decision means Marston's Pedigree and Bass Ale will no longer be brewed in Burton".

He added: "We must do everything we can to try and reverse this decision and look after all of the workers and their families."

title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
text:
Asos has told its customers hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and customer numbers are now in the hands of cyber criminals.

So too are the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.

With this information, scammers may be able to craft potent phishing attack emails or phone calls.

The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.

In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.

"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.

"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."

The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed."

The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording.

On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack.

The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first.

Asos said it is still investigating how the hack happened.

It told customers hackers "gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".

With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.

In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".

Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.

The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.

Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached.

Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action.

But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity.

Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information".

"We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.
